sec10-card-sec10-R06.expected_back: Other benefits listed are less congestion on the interstate, a sense of fairness because all lanes move at the same rate, and fewer road rage incidents.

sec10-card-sec10-R07.front: Under what traffic condition does moving over early beat waiting for a zipper merge?
sec10-card-sec10-R07.expected_back: When traffic is moving at highway speed with no backups, it makes sense to move over early to the lane that will stay open, and the bottom line is to merge when it is safe.

sec12-card-sec12-F01.front: What overriding safety duty rests on every driver regardless of who started a mistake?
sec12-card-sec12-F01.expected_back: Every driver has the responsibility to do everything possible to prevent collisions.

sec12-card-sec12-R01.front: Why should every driver rehearse emergency responses before trouble ever strikes?
sec12-card-sec12-R01.expected_back: Most drivers will face an emergency sooner or later, and being prepared may let you prevent a serious outcome.

sec12-card-sec12-F02.front: What are your exact three vehicle-control options to avoid a crash or soften its impact?
sec12-card-sec12-F02.expected_back: You have three options for avoiding a collision or reducing its impact: braking, steering or accelerating.

sec12-card-sec12-R02.front: Which of the three evasion moves is almost every driver's automatic first instinct?
sec12-card-sec12-R02.expected_back: For most drivers the first instinct when a collision threatens is to stop the vehicle.

sec12-card-sec12-F03.front: What two advantages does an anti-lock braking system give you during a hard emergency stop?
sec12-card-sec12-F03.expected_back: Most new vehicles have an anti-lock braking system, or ABS, which lets you stop without skidding while keeping steering control, so read your owner's manual on how to use it.

sec12-card-sec12-F04.front: How must your foot press an anti-lock brake pedal in an emergency—and why must you never pump it?
sec12-card-sec12-F04.expected_back: With ABS, press the brake pedal as hard as you can and hold constant pressure, and do not pump the brakes, because pumping deactivates ABS.

sec12-card-sec12-R03.front: How does proper anti-lock braking technique contrast directly against old-school pedal pumping?
sec12-card-sec12-R03.expected_back: ABS braking means firm, constant pressure on the pedal, the opposite of pumping, which would switch ABS off.

sec12-card-sec12-F05.front: What pedal feel and sound are completely normal while anti-lock brakes are actively working?
sec12-card-sec12-F05.expected_back: ABS works only while you keep pressure on the pedal, and a vibrating pedal or a clicking sound during ABS braking is normal.

sec12-card-sec12-F06.front: Can you steer around a hazard while holding full emergency pressure on anti-lock brakes?
sec12-card-sec12-F06.expected_back: You can still steer your vehicle while ABS is active.

sec12-card-sec12-R04.front: Where should you check the proper emergency-braking method if driving an older vehicle without anti-lock brakes?
sec12-card-sec12-R04.expected_back: If your vehicle has no ABS, follow your owner's manual for the right braking procedure.

sec12-card-sec12-F07.front: What maneuver is called swerving, and when does it outperform straight-line braking?
sec12-card-sec12-F07.expected_back: Quickly steering around a problem, sometimes called swerving, may let you avoid a collision.

sec12-card-sec12-F08.front: How should you grip the wheel and aim your car during the opening move of an emergency swerve?
sec12-card-sec12-F08.expected_back: To swerve, hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands and steer the way you want to go while trying to avoid other traffic.

sec12-card-sec12-F09.front: Once your vehicle clears the obstacle during a swerve, what counter-move restores smooth control?
sec12-card-sec12-F09.expected_back: Once past the problem, steer the opposite way to straighten the vehicle, regain control and settle at a suitable speed.

sec12-card-sec12-R05.front: What two linked steering cuts make up every controlled emergency swerve?
sec12-card-sec12-R05.expected_back: A swerve has two steering moves: first toward where you want to go, then back the opposite way to straighten out once the problem is cleared.

sec12-card-sec12-F10.front: Against threats coming from which two angles can accelerating save you from a collision?
sec12-card-sec12-F10.expected_back: Accelerating may be the way to avoid a collision, for example when another vehicle is about to hit you from behind or from the side.

sec12-card-sec12-R06.front: Why must you keep acceleration in your mental toolkit alongside braking and swerving?
sec12-card-sec12-R06.expected_back: Braking and swerving are not the only escapes, because speeding up may be what avoids a vehicle about to strike you from behind or the side.

sec12-card-sec12-F11.front: What three speed, braking, or traction conditions trigger a skid and strip away control?
sec12-card-sec12-F11.memory_hook: Excess speed, sudden stops, lost grip
sec12-card-sec12-F11.expected_back: Skids happen when you drive too fast for road conditions, stop suddenly or the tires can no longer grip the road, and once skidding you have little control.

sec12-card-sec12-F12.front: What three immediate foot, eye, and steering moves recover a skidding vehicle?
sec12-card-sec12-F12.expected_back: If your vehicle starts to skid, ease off the brake or accelerator, look where you want to go and steer in that direction.

sec12-card-sec12-F13.front: What dangerous reflex does the manual call panic steering when tires drop off an uneven pavement edge?
sec12-card-sec12-F13.expected_back: Avoid panic steering, which is trying to get back onto the pavement the instant the wheels leave it at an uneven drop-off.

sec12-card-sec12-F14.front: How should you bring your vehicle safely back onto the road after dropping off an uneven edge?
sec12-card-sec12-F14.expected_back: If an uneven drop-off takes your vehicle off the paved surface, slow down gradually when it is safe and steer gently back onto the pavement.

sec12-card-sec12-F15.front: Why do shallow angles and slight steering inputs matter whenever leaving or rejoining unpaved shoulders?
sec12-card-sec12-F15.expected_back: Going off and coming back onto the road gradually, with only slight steering, reduces the chance of erratic vehicle behavior on an uneven or unpaved shoulder.

sec12-card-sec12-R07.front: What turns a minor wheel drop off an uneven road edge into a severe collision?
sec12-card-sec12-R07.expected_back: Uneven surface drop-offs can cause serious collisions when a driver reacts the wrong way.

sec12-card-sec12-R09.front: How does the textbook drop-off recovery contrast directly with the dangerous reflex?
sec12-card-sec12-R09.expected_back: At a drop-off the safe response is a gradual slowdown and gentle steering back on, while the dangerous one is an immediate jerk back onto the pavement.

sec12-card-sec12-R08.front: What simple ownership habit sharply cuts your odds of facing a mechanical failure mid-trip?
sec12-card-sec12-R08.expected_back: Following the maintenance schedule in your owner's manual greatly cuts the chance of a vehicle problem while driving.

sec12-card-sec12-F16.front: What does a glowing brake warning lamp on your dash mean, and may you drive anyway?
sec12-card-sec12-F16.expected_back: Check all warning lights, including the brake light, because a brake warning light means the brakes are not working properly and you should not drive.

sec12-card-sec12-F17.front: If your regular foot brakes fail while moving, how do you apply the parking brake without skidding?
sec12-card-sec12-F17.expected_back: If the brakes fail while you drive, use the parking brake, pulling its handle or pushing its pedal slowly so the rear wheels do not lock, and be ready to release it if a skid starts.

sec12-card-sec12-F18.front: What must you do if both your regular brakes and your parking brake fail together?
sec12-card-sec12-F18.expected_back: If the parking brake does not work either, turn off the engine, find a safe place to slow to a stop off the roadway, and do not keep driving without working brakes.

sec12-card-sec12-R12.front: In South Carolina's brake-failure protocol, which backup comes first and which is the final fallback?
sec12-card-sec12-R12.expected_back: For brake failure the parking brake comes first, and turning off the engine is the fallback only if the parking brake also fails.

sec12-card-sec12-F19.front: What defines a tire blowout, and how does your vehicle react when a front tire blows?
sec12-card-sec12-F19.expected_back: A tire blowout is a rapid loss of air from a tire, and if a front tire blows out the vehicle pulls sharply toward the side of the blowout.

sec12-card-sec12-F20.front: What three sensations tell you a rear tire—rather than a front tire—just blew out?
sec12-card-sec12-F20.expected_back: If a rear tire blows out, the vehicle wobbles, shakes and pulls somewhat toward the side of the blowout.

sec12-card-sec12-R10.front: How do the steering pull and chassis feel contrast between a front blowout and a rear blowout?
sec12-card-sec12-R10.expected_back: A front tire blowout pulls the vehicle sharply toward the blown side, while a rear blowout makes it wobble and shake and pull only somewhat.

sec12-card-sec12-F21.front: What three immediate hand, steering, and throttle moves stabilize a sudden blowout or flat?
sec12-card-sec12-F21.memory_hook: Firm grip, hold straight, lift gas
sec12-card-sec12-F21.expected_back: In a blowout or sudden flat, grip the wheel firmly, keep the vehicle going straight and slow down gradually by taking your foot off the accelerator.

sec12-card-sec12-F22.front: Why should you stay off the brake pedal right after a tire blows out?
sec12-card-sec12-F22.expected_back: Do not brake after a blowout; let the vehicle slow on its own, or brake gently if you must.

sec12-card-sec12-F23.front: Where should you bring a blown-tire vehicle to a stop, and what lights go on immediately?
sec12-card-sec12-F23.expected_back: Avoid stopping on the road after a blowout if at all possible; pull off in a safe place, turn on the emergency flashers and have the tire changed and replaced.

sec12-card-sec12-R11.front: How does brake-pedal advice differ between a tire blowout and a sudden engine shutdown?
sec12-card-sec12-R11.expected_back: After a blowout you avoid braking and let the vehicle coast down, while after an engine failure you brake with steady pressure rather than hard.

sec12-card-sec12-F24.front: What happens to your steering effort if the engine dies mid-drive—and does the wheel lock up?
sec12-card-sec12-F24.expected_back: If the engine shuts off while driving, keep a strong grip, knowing the steering wheel may be hard to turn but can still be turned.

sec12-card-sec12-F25.front: After your engine cuts out while moving, how do you slow down and leave the road?
sec12-card-sec12-F25.expected_back: After an engine failure, look for an escape path and, instead of braking hard, use steady brake pressure to slow down and pull off the roadway.

sec12-card-sec12-F26.front: Once safely off the road after an engine failure, what restart check and three distress steps follow?
sec12-card-sec12-F26.expected_back: Once stopped after an engine failure, try to restart it, and if that fails, raise the hood, turn on the emergency flashers and call for help.

sec12-card-sec12-F27.front: In South Carolina's manual, what exact three-step sequence handles a vehicle accelerating out of control?
sec12-card-sec12-F27.expected_back: If your vehicle is accelerating out of control, the manual says to turn off the engine, shift to neutral and search for an escape path.

sec12-card-sec12-R13.front: How does post-stop advice after a stuck accelerator contrast against post-stop advice after an engine stall?
sec12-card-sec12-R13.expected_back: For a stuck accelerator the printed order is engine off, then neutral, then an escape path, which differs from the restart attempt used after an engine failure.

sec12-card-sec12-F28.front: How do you steer, brake, and handle repairs once you tame a stuck accelerator?
sec12-card-sec12-F28.expected_back: With a stuck accelerator, steer smoothly, brake gently, pull off the roadway and have the pedal repaired at a service center before driving again.

sec12-card-sec12-F29.front: Why is making a broken-down highway vehicle easy to spot from far back so critical?
sec12-card-sec12-F29.expected_back: If your vehicle breaks down on the highway, make sure others can see it, since collisions often happen when a driver notices a disabled vehicle too late to stop.

sec12-card-sec12-R14.front: Whose disabled vehicle should you report to authorities when you carry a cell phone?
sec12-card-sec12-R14.expected_back: If you have a cell phone or other device, use it to tell authorities that your vehicle, or another one, has broken down.

sec12-card-sec12-F30.front: What two immediate steps protect you whenever mechanical trouble forces a roadside stop?
sec12-card-sec12-F30.expected_back: If you must stop with vehicle trouble, get off the road and away from traffic if possible and turn on your emergency flashers.

sec12-card-sec12-F31.front: How many feet behind a disabled vehicle should emergency flares sit in South Carolina?
sec12-card-sec12-F31.expected_back: If you carry emergency flares, set them about two hundred to three hundred feet behind the vehicle so other drivers have time to change lanes.

sec12-card-sec12-R15.front: How do emergency flashers on your car and flares down the road split warning duties?
sec12-card-sec12-R15.expected_back: Flashers show your vehicle is disabled, while flares placed well behind it give approaching drivers time to change lanes.

sec12-card-sec12-F32.front: Which three credential holders can register emergency contacts online on their South Carolina motor vehicle record?
sec12-card-sec12-F32.expected_back: Holders of a beginner's permit, driver's license or identification card can enter emergency contact information on their SCDMV record through the dmv.sc.gov website.

sec12-card-sec12-F33.front: After a serious crash or medical emergency, who can view and share your registered emergency contact details?
sec12-card-sec12-F33.expected_back: After a collision or medical emergency, South Carolina law enforcement officers can then see that emergency contact information and may share it with medical personnel.

sec11-card-sec11-R01.front: What two real-world ingredients actually build safe, skillful driving over time?
sec11-card-sec11-R01.expected_back: Driving skills come only through practice and experience, and the manual offers these tips as things to practice to become a safer, more skillful driver.

sec11-card-sec11-F01.front: Which three zones around your vehicle must you monitor both before pulling out and while driving?
sec11-card-sec11-F01.expected_back: Before starting the vehicle and while driving, you must know what is happening around you by looking ahead, to the sides and behind.

sec11-card-sec11-F02.front: What visual routine should you build and run on every single trip behind the wheel?
sec11-card-sec11-F02.expected_back: Develop a searching pattern for your eyes and use it every time you drive.

sec11-card-sec11-F03.front: Why must your eyes keep sweeping across the scene rather than staring fixedly at one spot?
sec11-card-sec11-F03.expected_back: Searching shows you situations that could become a problem and gives you time to change your speed or road position, so keep your eyes moving instead of staring at any one thing.

sec11-card-sec11-F04.front: What three safety payoffs come from looking well down your intended travel path?
sec11-card-sec11-F04.expected_back: Looking well down your planned path gives you time to adjust and plan, leads to better decisions and may spare you from emergency braking and steering.

sec11-card-sec11-F05.front: In South Carolina, how many seconds ahead of your vehicle should you ideally scan?
sec11-card-sec11-F05.expected_back: Ideally, try to watch what is happening twenty to thirty seconds ahead of your vehicle.

sec11-card-sec11-F06.front: How do you keep tall vehicles ahead from cutting off your forward sight distance?
sec11-card-sec11-F06.expected_back: Avoid situations that cut how far you can see, such as following a larger vehicle too closely, and adjust your speed and road position to see best.

sec11-card-sec11-R02.front: How does downtown urban driving change how far ahead you can practically scan compared with open highways?
sec11-card-sec11-R02.expected_back: How far ahead you can look depends on where you drive, and in cities and urban areas you may not see as far as on a highway.

sec11-card-sec11-R03.front: What specific danger are you watching for when scanning to the left and right sides of your vehicle?
sec11-card-sec11-R03.expected_back: Search to the sides of your vehicle to see whether other road users are about to cross your path.

sec11-card-sec11-F07.front: During which four driving moments is checking your mirrors for rear traffic especially critical?
sec11-card-sec11-F07.expected_back: Stay aware of traffic behind you, using your mirrors, especially when you change lanes, slow down or stop, or enter an intersection.

sec11-card-sec11-F08.front: What three elements define driving at a genuinely safe speed?
sec11-card-sec11-F08.expected_back: Driving safely means adjusting your speed to road and traffic conditions, keeping an adequate following distance and obeying the speed limits that apply.

sec11-card-sec11-F09.front: When do you shed speed for a bend, and how do you use the gas pedal through the curve?
sec11-card-sec11-F09.expected_back: Always slow down before you enter a curve, to a safe speed that lets you apply slight and constant acceleration all the way through it.

sec11-card-sec11-F10.front: Which three road, traffic, or sightline factors call for dropping speed even lower before a curve?
sec11-card-sec11-F10.expected_back: Slow down even more on a curve when traction is poor, when you are following other vehicles and when you cannot see where the curve ends.

sec11-card-sec11-R04.front: Why must your braking finish on the straight approach rather than hard inside the curve?
sec11-card-sec11-R04.expected_back: Speed should come down before the curve, because hard braking after you have entered it could make the tires lose traction.

sec11-card-sec11-F11.front: How soon should you ease off your speed when rain, snow, sleet, or ice starts?
sec11-card-sec11-F11.expected_back: Reduce your speed at the first sign of rain, snow, sleet or ice.

sec11-card-sec11-F12.front: How does reduced tire grip on slippery pavement change both stopping and cornering?
sec11-card-sec11-F12.expected_back: On a slippery road your tires grip less, so stopping takes longer and turning without skidding is harder.

sec11-card-sec11-F13.front: What happens between your steering tires and wet asphalt during hydroplaning?
sec11-card-sec11-F13.expected_back: Hydroplaning is when your steering tires end up riding on a film of water above the road surface, much like water skis.

sec11-card-sec11-F14.front: What is the single best action to keep your tires from hydroplaning on wet or puddled roads?
sec11-card-sec11-F14.expected_back: The best way to avoid losing traction to hydroplaning is to slow down in the rain or on roads with pooled water or puddles.

sec11-card-sec11-F15.front: What must you do whenever you encounter floodwater over the roadway or flood barricades ahead?
sec11-card-sec11-F15.expected_back: If you see a flooded road, or barricades blocking one, find another route to where you are going.

sec11-card-sec11-F16.front: How quickly—and with how much warning—can flash floods strike after heavy rainfall?
sec11-card-sec11-F16.expected_back: Flash floods can come quickly and without warning, within a few minutes or hours of excessive rainfall.

sec11-card-sec11-R05.front: What four water sources trigger road flooding, and which three terrain spots collect floodwater first?
sec11-card-sec11-R05.expected_back: Flooding can come from rivers and streams overflowing, dams or levees breaking, run-off from deep snow or any heavy rainfall, and floodwater gathers on roads, bridges and low areas.

sec11-card-sec11-R06.front: Why do flood-prone roads demand extra caution after dark?
sec11-card-sec11-R06.expected_back: Take special care at night around possible flooding, when visibility is limited.

sec11-card-sec11-F17.front: How many inches of standing water reach the underside of most passenger cars to stall or spin them?
sec11-card-sec11-F17.expected_back: Six inches of water reaches the bottom of most passenger cars and can cause loss of control or stalling.

sec11-card-sec11-F18.front: What depth of moving water can sweep away nearly any vehicle—including pickups and sport utility vehicles?
sec11-card-sec11-F18.expected_back: Two feet of moving water can sweep away most vehicles, including sport utility vehicles and pickup trucks.

sec11-card-sec11-R07.front: How do the six-inch and two-foot floodwater thresholds escalate in danger?
sec11-card-sec11-R07.expected_back: Six inches of water is enough to reach the underside of most passenger cars, while two feet of moving water can carry away even SUVs and pickups.

sec11-card-sec11-F19.front: What two unseen roadway hazards make crossing even shallow-looking floodwater dangerous?
sec11-card-sec11-F19.expected_back: Never try to cross a flooded road even if it looks shallow, because the water can hide dips and other hazards and can wash away the road's underlying surface.

sec11-card-sec11-R08.front: What is your safest move if floodwater blocks every available route ahead and behind?
sec11-card-sec11-R08.expected_back: If no other route exists, drive to higher ground and wait for the floodwater to go down.

sec11-card-sec11-F20.front: From what mental moment to what physical finish does total stopping distance measure?
sec11-card-sec11-F20.expected_back: Total stopping distance is how far your vehicle travels, in ideal conditions, from the moment you realize you must stop until it actually stops.

sec11-card-sec11-F21.front: How does higher travel speed affect both the time and the pavement footage needed to stop?
sec11-card-sec11-F21.expected_back: The faster you are going, the more time and distance you need to stop.

sec11-card-sec11-F22.front: What happens during perception time, and what average fraction-to-whole second does it take an alert driver?
sec11-card-sec11-F22.expected_back: Perception time is the time and distance it takes to recognize that you must stop, and for an alert driver it averages three quarters second to one second.

sec11-card-sec11-F23.front: What physical action defines reaction time, and how long does it average?
sec11-card-sec11-F23.expected_back: Reaction time is the time and distance it takes to move your foot from the gas pedal and start braking, and it averages three quarters second to one second.

sec11-card-sec11-R09.front: How do perception time and reaction time differ in task while sharing the exact same average duration?
sec11-card-sec11-R09.expected_back: Perception time is about recognizing that you must stop, while reaction time is about moving your foot from the gas to the brake, and both average three quarters second to one second.

sec11-card-sec11-F24.front: What is mechanical braking distance—and roughly how many feet does it take at fifty miles per hour on dry pavement?
sec11-card-sec11-F24.expected_back: Braking distance is the time and distance your brakes need to stop the vehicle, about one hundred fifty-eight feet at fifty miles per hour on dry pavement with good brakes.

sec11-card-sec11-F25.front: What term describes the protective open buffer kept around every side of your car, and what does it buy?
sec11-card-sec11-F25.expected_back: The more space you leave between you and other road users, the more time you have to react; this space is called a space cushion, and you should keep one all around your vehicle.

sec11-card-sec11-F26.front: What two critical safety margins disappear whenever you follow the car ahead too closely?
sec11-card-sec11-F26.expected_back: Following the vehicle ahead too closely limits your view of the road and leaves too little time to react and avoid a collision.

sec11-card-sec11-F27.front: At least how many seconds of following distance should you maintain behind the vehicle ahead in South Carolina?
sec11-card-sec11-F27.expected_back: Always try to keep a following distance of at least four seconds behind the vehicle in front.

sec11-card-sec11-F28.front: How do you use a roadside pole or sign to measure your four-second following cushion?
sec11-card-sec11-F28.expected_back: To check the gap, note when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes a sign, pole or other fixed point, then count one thousand one, one thousand two and so on until you reach that point.

sec11-card-sec11-F29.front: What should you do if your nose reaches the landmark before finishing one thousand four?
sec11-card-sec11-F29.expected_back: If you reach the fixed point before counting to one thousand four, you are too close, so slow down and count again at another point until the gap is at least four seconds.

sec11-card-sec11-R10.front: How can you practice training your eyes to judge a four-second gap accurately?
sec11-card-sec11-R10.expected_back: You can test how well you judge the four-second gap by guessing how many seconds away an object is and then counting the seconds it takes to reach it.

sec11-card-sec11-F30.front: How must your following cushion change whenever pavement turns wet, icy, or slick?
sec11-card-sec11-F30.expected_back: Increase your following distance on slippery roads.

sec11-card-sec11-F31.front: In what visibility conditions—and behind which rail-stopping or oversize vehicles—should you add extra following distance?
sec11-card-sec11-F31.expected_back: Also leave more room at night, in fog or bad weather, behind vehicles that must stop at railroad crossings such as transit buses, school buses and hazardous materials carriers, and behind large vehicles like trucks, buses, RVs and vehicles towing trailers.

sec11-card-sec11-F32.front: What two hazards make cruising side-by-side next to another vehicle for miles a bad habit?
sec11-card-sec11-F32.expected_back: Avoid driving beside other vehicles for long stretches, because you may sit in their blind spot and lose the side space you might need to avoid a crash.

sec11-card-sec11-F33.front: How should you position your vehicle within your lane relative to the yellow centerline and oncoming traffic?
sec11-card-sec11-F33.expected_back: Do not crowd the centerline, and keep as much room as you can between you and oncoming traffic.

sec11-card-sec11-R11.front: What two cooperative moves help ramp traffic join a multi-lane or limited-access highway smoothly?
sec11-card-sec11-R11.expected_back: Make room for vehicles joining a multi-lane or limited access road by moving over a lane or adjusting your speed.

sec11-card-sec11-F34.front: Which three groups of people outside cars deserve an extra-wide space cushion?
sec11-card-sec11-F34.expected_back: Give pedestrians extra space, especially children, elderly people and bicyclists.

sec11-card-sec11-F35.front: Where inside your lane should you ease when a tractor-trailer overtakes you?
sec11-card-sec11-F35.expected_back: When a tractor trailer passes you, give it more room by moving to the outer part of your lane, away from the truck.

sec11-card-sec11-R12.front: What three smooth habits help the driver behind you maintain a safe following gap?
sec11-card-sec11-R12.memory_hook: Steady pace, early signals, forward cushion
sec11-card-sec11-R12.expected_back: You can help the driver behind you keep a safe distance by holding a steady speed, signaling early and leaving extra room ahead before you slow down or turn.

sec11-card-sec11-F36.front: Besides precipitation and dusk, what low-sun angle makes turning on headlights smart so others spot you?
sec11-card-sec11-F36.expected_back: Headlights help others see you, especially on rainy, snowy or foggy days, when you should use low beams and slow down, and as it gets dark or when you drive away from a rising or setting sun.

sec11-card-sec11-R14.front: Which headlight beam setting—paired with slower speed—belongs on rainy, snowy, or foggy days?
sec11-card-sec11-R14.expected_back: On rainy, snowy or foggy days the manual says to drive with your low-beam lights on and to slow down.

sec11-card-sec11-F37.front: In what three drift or inattention moments does a light tap on the horn help prevent trouble?
sec11-card-sec11-F37.expected_back: A light horn tap is useful when pedestrians or bicyclists seem to be moving into your lane, when you pass a driver who starts turning into your lane, or when a driver is not paying attention or may not see you.

sec11-card-sec11-R13.front: Under everyday driving conditions, how forceful should a warning sound on your horn be?
sec11-card-sec11-R13.expected_back: Under normal circumstances a light tap on the horn should be all you need.

sec11-card-sec11-F38.front: Why must you save the horn strictly for safety communication—and around whom must you never honk?
sec11-card-sec11-F38.expected_back: Use the horn only to communicate, since misuse can scare or anger other road users, and do not use it near blind pedestrians.

sec11-card-sec11-R16.front: Should you ever tap your horn to let a blind pedestrian know your car is waiting?
sec11-card-sec11-R16.expected_back: The horn is a tool for getting attention when needed, but near blind pedestrians it should not be used at all.

sec11-card-sec11-F39.front: How many feet in advance does South Carolina law require signaling before turns, lane changes, or merges?
sec11-card-sec11-F39.expected_back: South Carolina law requires a turn signal at least one hundred feet before you change lanes, turn left or right, or merge into traffic.

sec11-card-sec11-R15.front: Why must you verify your turn signal turns off right after finishing a merge, lane change, or gentle turn?
sec11-card-sec11-R15.expected_back: Once a lane change, turn or merge is finished, cancel your signal so other drivers are not confused.

sec11-card-sec11-F40.front: In what two road-exit or pre-corner situations should your blinker start even before you touch the brake?
sec11-card-sec11-F40.expected_back: Brake lights tell others you are slowing, and you should signal before slowing when turning off a road that has no separate turn or exit lane, or when parking or turning just before an intersection.

sec11-card-sec11-R17.front: Why aren't brake lights alone enough when turning off a highway that lacks a separate turn bay?
sec11-card-sec11-R17.expected_back: Brake lights show you are slowing, but you should also signal before slowing when you leave a road that has no separate turn or exit lane.

sec13-card-sec13-R01.front: How do courtesy and clear signaling protect everyone sharing the road?
sec13-card-sec13-R01.expected_back: Be courteous and let other road users know where you are and what you plan to do, which helps avoid collisions.

sec13-card-sec13-R02.front: What two visibility and behavior challenges make pedestrians extra risky around traffic?
sec13-card-sec13-R02.expected_back: Pedestrians are hard to see, and it is hard to tell what they intend to do.

sec13-card-sec13-F01.front: How must you respond to a pedestrian stepping into the street outside a crosswalk?
sec13-card-sec13-F01.expected_back: Always be prepared to yield to pedestrians, even when they are not in a crosswalk.

sec13-card-sec13-F02.front: Which unpainted or mid-street pedestrian crossings still require you to yield the right-of-way?
sec13-card-sec13-F02.expected_back: You must yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk even if it is unmarked, and that includes mid-block crosswalks shown by warning signs and pavement markings.

sec13-card-sec13-R03.front: Contrast your legal obligation toward a pedestrian outside a crosswalk versus inside any marked or unmarked crosswalk?
sec13-card-sec13-R03.expected_back: Outside a crosswalk you must be prepared to yield to pedestrians, while inside any crosswalk, marked or not, you are required to yield.

sec13-card-sec13-F03.front: What exact action is required when a visually impaired pedestrian crosses with a guide dog or white cane?
sec13-card-sec13-F03.expected_back: You must always yield the right-of-way to visually impaired people, and you must come to a complete stop when a pedestrian crosses guided by a dog or carrying a white cane.

sec13-card-sec13-R04.front: Which specific pedestrian cues upgrade your normal duty to yield into a mandatory complete stop?
sec13-card-sec13-R04.expected_back: For most pedestrians the duty is to yield, but a pedestrian crossing with a guide dog or a white cane requires a complete stop.

sec13-card-sec13-F04.front: Does a fresh green traffic light give you right-of-way over pedestrians still crossing the intersection?
sec13-card-sec13-F04.expected_back: Yield the right-of-way to every pedestrian in the intersection, even when your light is green.

sec13-card-sec13-F05.front: While looking left for oncoming cars on a right-on-red turn, whom must you stay ready to yield to?
sec13-card-sec13-F05.expected_back: When turning right on red, be ready to yield the right-of-way to pedestrians.

sec13-card-sec13-F06.front: How should you handle passing a stopped vehicle or driving alongside a row of parked cars?
sec13-card-sec13-F06.expected_back: Beside parked or stopped vehicles, pedestrians can step out between them, so slow down and do not pass a stopped vehicle until you are sure no one is crossing in front of it.

sec13-card-sec13-F07.front: Before shifting into reverse—especially in busy parking lots—what path check comes first?
sec13-card-sec13-F07.expected_back: Before backing up, check for pedestrians in your path, especially in parking lots and other busy pedestrian areas.

sec13-card-sec13-F08.front: How should you adjust your speed near playgrounds and residential streets lined with parked cars?
sec13-card-sec13-F08.expected_back: In playground and residential areas children may run out from between parked vehicles, so it is wise to drive below the speed limit there and be ready to stop quickly.

sec13-card-sec13-F09.front: Under what conditions does a school-zone speed limit take effect, and how do you respond to a school traffic patrol?
sec13-card-sec13-F09.expected_back: In a school zone you must obey the lower speed limit when its lights are flashing or children are present, and at a school crossing with a traffic patrol you stop and yield if signaled.

sec13-card-sec13-R05.front: Must school-zone beacons be flashing AND children be outside together before the reduced speed limit applies?
sec13-card-sec13-R05.expected_back: The school zone speed limit applies either when its lights are flashing or when children are present, not only when both are true.

sec13-card-sec13-F10.front: How does South Carolina traffic law classify a bicycle riding on the roadway?
sec13-card-sec13-F10.expected_back: On the road a bicycle counts as a vehicle, so bicyclists must follow the same rules of the road and have the same rights, privileges and responsibilities as motorists.

sec13-card-sec13-R06.front: Why do approaching motorists need extra alertness around bicyclists in traffic?
sec13-card-sec13-R06.expected_back: Bicyclists may not be easy to spot in traffic, so stay alert and take extra care when approaching them.

sec13-card-sec13-F11.front: How does an unskillful bicyclist's riding differ from a skillful cyclist's steady line?
sec13-card-sec13-F11.expected_back: A skillful bicyclist rides predictably in a steady line, while an unskillful one may swerve, ignore signs and signals or ride at night without a light, so be ready for sudden moves.

sec13-card-sec13-R07.front: Which type of bicyclist is most likely to swerve unexpectedly into your path?
sec13-card-sec13-R07.expected_back: Like drivers, bicyclists have different skill levels, and the unskillful rider is the one to expect sudden swerves from.

sec13-card-sec13-F12.front: How much right-of-way must you grant a bicyclist riding through an intersection?
sec13-card-sec13-F12.expected_back: Yield to bicyclists in intersections just as you would to pedestrians and other vehicles.

sec13-card-sec13-F13.front: Besides yielding at bike-path crossings, which four narrow exceptions ever let a car enter or stop in a bike lane?
sec13-card-sec13-F13.expected_back: Yield where a bike path or lane crosses a road, and do not stop, park or drive in a bike lane unless entering or leaving an alley or driveway, on official duty, directed by police or in an emergency.

sec13-card-sec13-F14.front: How should you pass a bicyclist or time an intersection turn near one?
sec13-card-sec13-F14.expected_back: Give a bicyclist as much room as possible and slow down when approaching or passing, and let the cyclist clear the intersection before you make your turn.

sec13-card-sec13-F15.front: Why must you avoid braking abruptly right in front of a bicyclist?
sec13-card-sec13-F15.expected_back: Avoid slowing down or stopping suddenly near a bicyclist, because a motor vehicle's brakes are stronger than a bicycle's and you could cause a collision.

sec13-card-sec13-F16.front: When is sounding your horn close to a bicyclist justified, and why is casual honking dangerous?
sec13-card-sec13-F16.expected_back: Do not sound your horn close to a bicyclist unless a collision is possible, since the noise can startle the rider into steering into your path.

sec13-card-sec13-R08.front: Should you tap your horn behind a bicyclist just to announce that you are about to pass?
sec13-card-sec13-R08.expected_back: The horn near a bicyclist is reserved for a real chance of collision, not for simply announcing that you are there.

sec13-card-sec13-F17.front: Why do children riding bicycles on a sidewalk demand extra roadway vigilance?
sec13-card-sec13-F17.expected_back: Watch for bicyclists moving into your lane, and take special care when children ride on the sidewalk, because they may come onto the road.

sec13-card-sec13-F18.front: What two turning or lane-squeezing moves are forbidden around a bicyclist?
sec13-card-sec13-F18.expected_back: Do not turn sharply in front of a bicyclist, and never force one off the road.

sec13-card-sec13-F19.front: Even though cyclists must ride with traffic flow, where should drivers scan for them?
sec13-card-sec13-F19.expected_back: Bicyclists are required to ride with the direction of traffic, but you should still look for them anywhere on the roadway.

sec13-card-sec13-F20.front: Which three road-surface conditions destabilize bicycles far worse than four-wheeled cars?
sec13-card-sec13-F20.expected_back: Be extra careful around bicyclists on wet roads or roads covered with sand or gravel, which affect bicycles far more than cars.

sec13-card-sec13-F21.front: If a bicyclist keeps both hands on the bars instead of hand-signaling, what body cues warn of a move?
sec13-card-sec13-F21.expected_back: Bicyclists must use hand signals to turn and stop, but some may not know them or may need both hands on the handlebars, so watch for clues such as a head turn or a look over the shoulder.

sec13-card-sec13-F22.front: After parallel parking on a street, what check comes before swinging your car door open?
sec13-card-sec13-F22.expected_back: When parked on the street, check the sides and rear for bicyclists before you open your door.

sec13-card-sec13-R09.front: Where is checking behind your vehicle for bicyclists before backing up especially critical?
sec13-card-sec13-R09.expected_back: Check for bicyclists in your path before backing up, especially near schools and in residential areas where they are more likely.

sec13-card-sec13-F23.front: What legal rights and duties do motorcyclists carry, and what visibility challenge comes with them?
sec13-card-sec13-F23.expected_back: Motorcyclists have the same rights and responsibilities as other drivers, but they can be harder to see.

sec13-card-sec13-F24.front: May a car squeeze alongside a motorcycle inside the same traffic lane?
sec13-card-sec13-F24.expected_back: Give a motorcycle a full lane width and do not share the lane, because the rider needs that space to react to traffic.

sec13-card-sec13-F25.front: Because a motorcycle's narrow profile hides easily, which two checks belong before every lane move?
sec13-card-sec13-F25.expected_back: Motorcycles are small and hard to see, so remember they are part of traffic and always check your mirrors and blind spots for them.

sec13-card-sec13-F26.front: Where must you look carefully for motorcycles right before turning left?
sec13-card-sec13-F26.expected_back: Before turning left, look carefully to the front and sides of your vehicle for motorcycles.

sec13-card-sec13-F27.front: Why shouldn't you pull out in front of a motorcycle just because its turn signal is blinking?
sec13-card-sec13-F27.expected_back: Do not assume a motorcycle is turning just because its signal is flashing, since motorcycle signals may not cancel themselves; wait until you are sure the rider is turning.

sec13-card-sec13-F28.front: What minimum following time must you keep behind a motorcycle, and how does rain affect it?
sec13-card-sec13-F28.memory_hook: At least four seconds; wetter longer
sec13-card-sec13-F28.expected_back: Follow a motorcycle by at least four seconds, and by more in wet conditions, or you may lack the time and space to avoid a collision.

sec13-card-sec13-R11.front: Is a four-second following gap behind a motorcycle enough when pavement turns wet?
sec13-card-sec13-R11.expected_back: The four-second gap behind a motorcycle is a minimum, and wet conditions call for more.

sec13-card-sec13-F29.front: Which six minor pavement features can force a motorcyclist to swerve or slow abruptly?
sec13-card-sec13-F29.memory_hook: Gravel, potholes, tracks, grooves, seams, wet
sec13-card-sec13-F29.expected_back: Riders may suddenly change speed or lane position to avoid hazards such as gravel, potholes, railroad crossings, grooved pavement, pavement seams and wet or slippery surfaces, any of which can be deadly to them.

sec13-card-sec13-R10.front: How does the travel speed of scooters and mopeds compare against full-size motorcycles?
sec13-card-sec13-R10.expected_back: Scooters and mopeds travel much more slowly than motorcycles.

sec13-card-sec13-F30.front: Roughly how many collisions between passenger cars and commercial vehicles happen every year?
sec13-card-sec13-F30.expected_back: The manual reports more than two hundred fifty thousand collisions between cars and commercial vehicles each year, many of which could be avoided.

sec13-card-sec13-F31.front: In what four handling and visibility ways do commercial trucks differ from passenger cars?
sec13-card-sec13-F31.memory_hook: Bigger spots, longer stops, wider turns
sec13-card-sec13-F31.expected_back: Commercial vehicles are larger and harder to maneuver than cars, have much larger blind spots, need longer distances to stop and speed up, and need more room to turn.

sec13-card-sec13-F32.front: What is a commercial vehicle's no zone, and around which parts of a truck or bus does it sit?
sec13-card-sec13-F32.expected_back: The no zone is the area around large trucks and buses where other vehicles disappear from the driver's view, with blind spots at the sides, rear and front.

sec13-card-sec13-R13.front: Are truck and bus no zones found only along the left and right trailer sides?
sec13-card-sec13-R13.expected_back: No zones exist at the front and rear of large trucks and buses as well as on their sides.

sec13-card-sec13-F33.front: How far back does a large truck's right-side blind spot stretch from behind the cab?
sec13-card-sec13-F33.expected_back: Side no zones are big on both sides of large trucks and buses, and a truck's right-side blind spot starts behind the cab and can extend the length of the truck.

sec13-card-sec13-R12.front: Which side of a commercial truck carries the larger, more dangerous blind spot?
sec13-card-sec13-R12.expected_back: A truck's blind spot is larger on its right side than its left, starting behind the cab and reaching up to the truck's length.

sec13-card-sec13-F34.front: What quick visual check tells you whether a truck driver can spot your car?
sec13-card-sec13-F34.expected_back: If you cannot see the truck driver's face in the side view mirror, the driver cannot see you.

sec13-card-sec13-F35.front: Why shouldn't you cruise alongside a large truck or bus any longer than necessary?
sec13-card-sec13-F35.expected_back: Never stay alongside a large vehicle longer than you must, because if its driver has to swerve or change lanes the chance of a collision rises sharply.

sec15-card-sec15-F01.front: What basic visibility limit makes driving at night more dangerous than daytime driving?
sec15-card-sec15-F01.expected_back: Night driving is harder and more dangerous than daytime driving, because your headlights limit how far ahead you can see.

sec15-card-sec15-F02.front: When should you switch on high beams at night, and how much farther do they reach than low beams?
sec15-card-sec15-F02.expected_back: Use your high beams whenever there are no oncoming vehicles, since they let you see twice as far as low beams.

sec15-card-sec15-F03.front: Before an oncoming vehicle reaches within what distance must you dim your high beams?
sec15-card-sec15-F03.expected_back: Lower your high beams while an oncoming vehicle is still at least five hundred feet away.

sec15-card-sec15-F04.front: Where should you shift your gaze if an oncoming driver forgets to dim bright high beams?
sec15-card-sec15-F04.expected_back: If an oncoming vehicle keeps its high beams on, glance toward the right side of the road so you are not distracted or briefly blinded.

sec15-card-sec15-F05.front: Within how many feet behind another vehicle must you switch from high beams to low beams?
sec15-card-sec15-F05.expected_back: Use low beams when you are following another vehicle that is less than two hundred feet ahead of you.

sec15-card-sec15-F06.front: Why must you run low beams—and fog lights if equipped—instead of high beams in fog, rain, or snow?
sec15-card-sec15-F06.expected_back: In fog, rain or snow use low beams, because high beams can cause glare that makes it harder to see; some vehicles also have fog lights for these conditions.

sec15-card-sec15-F07.front: Instead of staring into oncoming headlights at night, what should your eyes keep doing?
sec15-card-sec15-F07.expected_back: Do not look straight into oncoming headlights; keep your eyes searching the road in front of you.

sec15-card-sec15-F08.front: How should you scan ahead and to the sides when driving after dark?
sec15-card-sec15-F08.expected_back: At night, search well beyond your headlight beams for dark shapes on the road, and glance left and right now and then to find the pavement edge and any hazards from the sides.

sec15-card-sec15-F09.front: Why must you never wear sunglasses or colored lenses at night or under overcast skies?
sec15-card-sec15-F09.memory_hook: Skip tinted lenses in low light
sec15-card-sec15-F09.expected_back: Do not wear sunglasses or colored lenses at night or on overcast days, because tinted lenses reduce your vision.

sec15-card-sec15-R01.front: Compare how many extra following seconds night driving adds on familiar roads versus unfamiliar roads?
sec15-card-sec15-R01.expected_back: Night driving alone calls for at least one added second of following time, while unfamiliar roads at night call for at least two.

sec15-card-sec15-F10.front: How many minimum extra seconds should you add to your following gap after dark and on unfamiliar night roads?
sec15-card-sec15-F10.expected_back: At night add at least one extra second to your following distance, and at least two extra seconds on unfamiliar roads at night.

sec15-card-sec15-F11.front: What three traffic disruptions commonly appear inside a highway work zone?
sec15-card-sec15-F11.expected_back: A work zone is an area where roadwork is under way, and it may involve a lane closure, a detour and moving equipment.

sec15-card-sec15-F12.front: Roughly how many people are injured every year in motor vehicle crashes inside work zones?
sec15-card-sec15-F12.expected_back: The manual says approximately forty thousand people a year are injured in motor vehicle collisions in work zones.

sec15-card-sec15-F13.front: What background and legend colors mark work-zone signs, and what five things should you watch for approaching?
sec15-card-sec15-F13.expected_back: Approaching a work zone, watch for signs, cones, barrels, large vehicles and workers, and remember that work zone signs have orange backgrounds with black letters or symbols.

sec15-card-sec15-F14.front: Why must you still slow down through a work zone when zero crew members are on site?
sec15-card-sec15-F14.memory_hook: Slow down; narrow rough lanes remain
sec15-card-sec15-F14.expected_back: Always slow down in a work zone even when no workers are present, because narrower lanes and rough pavement can make conditions hazardous.

sec15-card-sec15-F15.front: What two penalties hit your wallet and license record for endangering a South Carolina highway worker?
sec15-card-sec15-F15.expected_back: Endangering a highway worker can bring a fine and points on your driving record, under SC Code §fifty-six-five-one thousand five hundred thirty-five.

sec15-card-sec15-F16.front: Which four speed, spacing, scanning, and braking habits carry you safely through a work zone?
sec15-card-sec15-F16.expected_back: In a work zone, slow down, leave a longer following gap, keep track of surrounding traffic and be ready to stop.

sec15-card-sec15-F17.front: How carefully should you drive through a nighttime work zone when no crew appears present?
sec15-card-sec15-F17.expected_back: Use extreme caution in a work zone at night, whether or not workers are present.

sec15-card-sec15-F18.front: How should you position your car near crews, and what sign finally releases work-zone rules?
sec15-card-sec15-F18.expected_back: Shift your lane position to give workers and construction vehicles room, and keep obeying work zone signs until you see End Road Work.

sec15-card-sec15-R02.front: What two trip-planning habits keep highway roadwork from making you rush?
sec15-card-sec15-R02.expected_back: Expect work zone delays and plan for them by leaving earlier, and use alternate routes to avoid work zones when you can.

sec15-card-sec15-F19.front: What three core habits keep you safe on rural South Carolina roads?
sec15-card-sec15-F19.memory_hook: Stay alert, read warnings, obey limits
sec15-card-sec15-F19.expected_back: On rural roads stay alert, watch for warning signs and obey the speed limit.

sec15-card-sec15-F20.front: How do unpaved dirt and gravel roads change traction, spacing, and braking?
sec15-card-sec15-F20.expected_back: Gravel and dirt roads reduce traction, so slow down, leave more following distance and expect that you may skid when you stop.

sec15-card-sec15-F21.front: Where do you position your car on narrow country roads bordered by ditches or drop-offs?
sec15-card-sec15-F21.expected_back: Rural roads are often narrower, with ditches or drop-offs instead of shoulders, so slow down, keep centered in your lane and watch for oncoming traffic that may drift into it.

sec15-card-sec15-F22.front: How do drivers share a single-lane rural bridge, and who generally holds right-of-way?
sec15-card-sec15-F22.expected_back: At narrow or single-lane bridges drivers take turns, and generally the first driver to reach the bridge has the right-of-way.

sec15-card-sec15-F23.front: What three adjustments help you cross slippery steel bridges or open metal gratings?
sec15-card-sec15-F23.expected_back: Open bridge gratings and steel bridges can reduce traction, so slow down, increase your following distance and hold the wheel firmly.

sec15-card-sec15-F24.front: How must you approach rural curves or hillcrests blinded by woods or tall crops?
sec15-card-sec15-F24.expected_back: Blind corners created by woods, growing crops or steep hills limit how far you can see, so always slow down there and be ready to stop.

sec15-card-sec15-F25.front: How should you approach a rural crossroads that has neither stop nor yield signs?
sec15-card-sec15-F25.expected_back: Some rural intersections have no stop or yield signs, so approach them slowly and be ready to stop for crossing or oncoming traffic.

sec15-card-sec15-F26.front: Which four driver inputs must all slow down when rare snow or ice hits South Carolina?
sec15-card-sec15-F26.expected_back: South Carolina rarely has extreme winters but sometimes gets snow and ice, which call for slower speeds, acceleration, steering and braking.

sec15-card-sec15-F27.front: Which three road locations freeze earliest, and where can ice linger even above freezing?
sec15-card-sec15-F27.expected_back: Bridges, overpasses and lightly traveled roads tend to freeze first, and even above freezing, wet conditions can leave ice in shady spots or on exposed roads such as bridges.

sec15-card-sec15-F28.front: What tire equipment and glass prep does the manual recommend if you must drive in snow or ice?
sec15-card-sec15-F28.expected_back: If you must drive in snow or ice, tire chains or special snow tires are recommended, and you should keep the windshield and windows clear and use the defroster.

sec15-card-sec15-R03.front: What quick hand check confirms your windshield defroster actually blows air?
sec15-card-sec15-R03.expected_back: Check that the defroster works by turning on the fan and placing your hand on the dashboard.

sec15-card-sec15-F29.front: How can you help a rear-wheel-drive car bite better on slick winter pavement?
sec15-card-sec15-F29.expected_back: Extra weight loaded in the trunk can help a rear-wheel-drive car get traction.

sec15-card-sec15-F30.front: Why should you keep your gas tank full during freezing winter weather?
sec15-card-sec15-F30.expected_back: Keep a full tank of gasoline in winter to prevent condensation inside the tank, which may freeze.

sec15-card-sec15-F32.front: Should you engage cruise control when driving in wintry or icy conditions?
sec15-card-sec15-F32.expected_back: Avoid using cruise control in winter driving conditions.

sec15-card-sec15-F31.front: Where in the lane should you steer on snowy roads, and how should you apply the brakes?
sec15-card-sec15-F31.expected_back: When you can, drive in the tracks left by earlier vehicles, and brake gently to slow down or stop on snow or ice.

sec15-card-sec15-F33.front: Why must you keep extra winter spacing even after main road pavement looks clear?
sec15-card-sec15-F33.expected_back: Leave extra room between you and other vehicles on snow or ice, remembering that ice patches may form on bridges even when the roads are clear.

sec15-card-sec15-F34.front: If you cannot avoid a hill in winter, how should you climb it and why must you avoid stopping?
sec15-card-sec15-F34.expected_back: Generally avoid hills in winter, and if you must use them, drive slowly at a steady pace with a good gap ahead, since restarting after stopping on a hill may be nearly impossible.

sec15-card-sec15-F35.front: What steering, throttle, and shoveling steps free a snow-stuck car—and what wheel mistake digs you deeper?
sec15-card-sec15-F35.expected_back: If your vehicle gets stuck in snow, do not spin the wheels; turn them from side to side a few times, use a light touch on the gas and shovel snow away from the wheels and underside.

sec15-card-sec15-R04.front: Which seven household or roadside materials can give spinning tires bite when stuck in snow?
sec15-card-sec15-R04.expected_back: To get traction when stuck, pour sand, cat litter, gravel or salt in the wheels' path, or try cardboard, newspaper or brush under the wheels.

sec15-card-sec15-F36.front: What immediate pedal and steering move recovers a car skidding on snow or ice?
sec15-card-sec15-F36.expected_back: If your vehicle skids on winter roads, lift your foot off the accelerator and steer toward where you want the front of the vehicle to go.

sec15-card-sec15-R05.front: Contrast how you brake during a winter skid with anti-lock brakes versus non-ABS standard brakes?
sec15-card-sec15-R05.expected_back: In a winter skid with ABS, do not pump the brakes but hold steady pressure and expect the pedal to pulse, while with standard brakes you pump them gently.

sec15-card-sec15-R06.front: What does the manual say about leaving your vehicle sitting in the roadway during winter weather?
sec15-card-sec15-R06.expected_back: If at all possible, do not abandon your vehicle in the roadway.

sec15-card-sec15-R07.front: How widely are trailers towed each year even though individual drivers may tow only occasionally?
sec15-card-sec15-R07.expected_back: The manual notes that trailers are towed billions of miles every year, making towing a common everyday activity even if any one person does it only now and then.

sec15-card-sec15-R08.front: What factor contributes to the vast majority of crashes involving cars pulling trailers?
sec15-card-sec15-R08.expected_back: Your judgment and common sense are key to safe trailering, and driver error contributes to the large majority of crashes involving vehicle-trailer combinations.

sec15-card-sec15-R09.front: Which three connections complete a trailer hookup, and why shouldn't you stop mid-process?
sec15-card-sec15-R09.expected_back: Learn the correct hookup for your vehicle and trailer: couple the trailer to the hitch ball, hook up the safety chains and plug in the trailer lights, and finish the whole process without stopping to do something else.

sec15-card-sec15-R10.front: Right before pulling out with a trailer, what hitch connection and mirror condition must you verify?
sec15-card-sec15-R10.expected_back: Before leaving, check that the coupler and hitch ball are properly connected, and make sure both side mirrors are clean and undamaged.

sec15-card-sec15-F37.front: Which end of a trailer must carry more weight, and what happens when you load it backward?
sec15-card-sec15-F37.expected_back: Load a trailer heavier in the front to reduce sway, since failing to do so is a leading cause of vehicle-trailer mishaps.

sec15-card-sec15-F38.front: What exact front-to-rear percentage split governs loading cargo onto a trailer?
sec15-card-sec15-F38.expected_back: Put sixty percent of a trailer's cargo weight up front, closest to the towing vehicle, and the remaining forty percent toward the rear.

sec15-card-sec15-R11.front: After pulling over from trailer sway, how should you rebalance cargo and place heavy items?
sec15-card-sec15-R11.expected_back: After a sway, check that the cargo is heavier in front and reload if needed, keeping heavy items on the trailer floor rather than stacked on other items.

sec15-card-sec15-R12.front: How do you prevent shifting inside a partially loaded trailer, and what weight ceiling applies?
sec15-card-sec15-R12.expected_back: Pack cargo tightly, secure partial loads with tie-downs or straps and packing material, and never exceed the trailer maker's maximum gross weight.

sec15-card-sec15-F39.front: If your trailer starts swaying or whipping at speed, what should you do—and never do?
sec15-card-sec15-F39.memory_hook: Steer straight, ease off; don't brake
sec15-card-sec15-F39.expected_back: If a trailer starts to sway or whip, steer straight and slow down gradually without braking, never speed up, and stop once you can get completely off the road.

sec15-card-sec15-F40.front: What maximum speed does the manual recommend for most vehicle-trailer rigs?
sec15-card-sec15-F40.expected_back: The maximum recommended speed for most vehicle-trailer combinations is fifty-five miles per hour, the posted limit must never be exceeded, and worse conditions call for even lower speeds.

sec15-card-sec15-R13.front: What two practical payoffs come from accepting a slower pace whenever you tow?
sec15-card-sec15-R13.expected_back: Towing calls for adjusting your driving to the vehicle, accepting a slower pace, which also saves fuel and lowers the chance of losing control.

sec15-card-sec15-R14.front: At what point on a downhill grade must you shed speed when pulling a trailer?
sec15-card-sec15-R14.expected_back: Slow down before you start down a grade with a trailer, not after.

sec15-card-sec15-R15.front: How does hitching a trailer change your stopping distance, passing room, and bad-weather spacing?
sec15-card-sec15-R15.memory_hook: Longer stops, passes; double weather care
sec15-card-sec15-R15.expected_back: A vehicle with a trailer needs more distance to stop and more time and distance to pass, so leave extra space ahead, and even more in rain, snow or fog.

sec15-card-sec15-R16.front: Where must you never pass while towing, and why do corners require wider turns?
sec15-card-sec15-R16.expected_back: With a trailer, never pass on hills or curves, and remember the trailer does not follow directly behind the car, so turns need extra room.

sec15-card-sec15-F41.front: Where do you grip the steering wheel to back a trailer, and which way does your hand move?
sec15-card-sec15-F41.expected_back: When backing a trailer, go slowly with your hand at the bottom of the steering wheel, moving your hand left to send the trailer left and right to send it right.

sec15-card-sec15-F42.front: What three-step reset fixes a trailer that starts jackknifing while you back up?
sec15-card-sec15-F42.expected_back: If the trailer starts to jackknife, stop, pull ahead to straighten out and then start backing again.

sec15-card-sec15-R17.front: Whom should you consult whenever you feel unsure about hitching, loading, or towing a trailer?
sec15-card-sec15-R17.expected_back: If you are unsure how to hook up, load or drive with a trailer, get advice from a trailer professional.

sec15-card-sec15-R18.front: When should you walk around your rig, and which four items get rechecked every time?
sec15-card-sec15-R18.memory_hook: Fuel stops; hitch, chains, lights, tires
sec15-card-sec15-R18.expected_back: Before driving and at every fuel stop, walk around the rig and recheck the hitch and coupler tightness, safety chains, lights and tire pressures.

sec15-card-sec15-R19.front: How should you respond if an unfamiliar rattle or wobble starts while towing?
sec15-card-sec15-R19.expected_back: If you hear an unusual noise or suspect trouble while towing, stop at a safe place off the road to check it.

sec15-card-sec15-R20.front: How should you schedule long trailer trips instead of marathoning straight through?
sec15-card-sec15-R20.expected_back: On long trips, plan rest stops instead of driving straight through, so you drive in daylight while rested and alert.

sec15-card-sec15-R21.front: Which hardware, cargo, speed, inspection, and personal-safety items round out the manual's trailering checklist?
sec15-card-sec15-R21.expected_back: The safe trailering checklist covers a front-heavy load, a tight hitch, attached chains, working lights, correct tire pressures, reduced speed, thinking ahead, frequent rest, frequent inspection, a secure load and wearing your seat belt.

sec04-card-sec04-F01.front: What two foundations keep driving safe, and how risky does the manual rate getting behind the wheel?
sec04-card-sec04-F01.expected_back: Safe driving depends on good health and making correct decisions, and the manual calls driving one of the riskiest activities you may choose.

sec04-card-sec04-F02.front: Why is clear eyesight vital at the wheel, and what routine care does the manual recommend?
sec04-card-sec04-F02.expected_back: Without clear vision you struggle to identify traffic and road conditions, spot trouble and respond in time, so regular eye checks by a licensed eye care professional are advised.

sec04-card-sec04-F03.front: What must you do when corrective lenses are required, and what eyewear should stay off after dark?
sec04-card-sec04-F03.expected_back: If corrective lenses are required, always wear them when driving and avoid dark or tinted lenses at night, because they cut the light you need to see.

sec04-card-sec04-F04.front: Which form must drivers with bioptic telescopic lenses send in every year, and where does it go?
sec04-card-sec04-F04.expected_back: Drivers who use bioptic telescopic lenses must send the Low Vision Acuity Screening form four hundred twelve-LV to the SCDMV Driver Improvement unit every year.

sec04-card-sec04-R01.front: How often must bioptic telescopic lens users submit their low-vision acuity screening form to Driver Improvement?
sec04-card-sec04-R01.expected_back: Bioptic telescopic lens users file the Low Vision Acuity Screening, form four hundred twelve-LV, with the SCDMV Driver Improvement unit every year, so their screening is an annual filing.

sec04-card-sec04-F05.front: What two options do you have for getting your distance eyesight checked for licensing?
sec04-card-sec04-F05.expected_back: Vision can be tested at a branch with an orthorater, a device that checks how well you read at a distance, or by a licensed eye care professional.

sec04-card-sec04-F06.front: In what two situations must a licensed eye care professional check your eyesight?
sec04-card-sec04-F06.expected_back: A licensed eye care professional must test you if you fail the SCDMV vision test or choose not to be tested at the branch.

sec04-card-sec04-R04.front: Must every applicant use the branch vision machine first, or can you go straight to an eye specialist?
sec04-card-sec04-R04.expected_back: Branch testing is optional: you may skip it and go straight to a licensed eye care professional, who must also test you if you fail the branch test.

sec04-card-sec04-F07.front: How does submitting a vision certificate differ between South Carolina eye specialists and out-of-state specialists?
sec04-card-sec04-F07.expected_back: SC-licensed eye care professionals submit the Certificate of Vision Examination online, while out-of-state professionals complete SCDMV Form four hundred twelve-NC.

sec04-card-sec04-R02.front: Which vision specialist files electronically through the online portal, and which completes Form four-twelve-NC?
sec04-card-sec04-R02.expected_back: A South Carolina-licensed eye care professional must submit the Certificate of Vision Examination electronically through SCDMV's online portal, whereas an out-of-state professional must complete SCDMV Form four-twelve-NC.

sec04-card-sec04-F08.front: Which four licensing events require you to complete a vision screening in South Carolina?
sec04-card-sec04-F08.expected_back: Vision screening is required for a first SC permit or license, to remove corrective lens restriction code A, for renewals of a license or permit since October one, two thousand twenty, and when surrendering an out-of-state license.

sec04-card-sec04-F09.front: How many months does a standard vision screening certificate stay valid under the rule starting May two thousand twenty-four?
sec04-card-sec04-F09.expected_back: From May eighteen, two thousand twenty-four, standard vision screening certificates stay valid for thirty-six months.

sec04-card-sec04-F10.front: What is the minimum corrected eyesight standard required to pass screening in South Carolina?
sec04-card-sec04-F10.expected_back: The minimum vision standard is no stricter than twenty over forty corrected in one eye.

sec04-card-sec04-F11.front: What happens to your permit or license if you need glasses or contacts to meet the vision standard?
sec04-card-sec04-F11.expected_back: If you meet the standard only with glasses or contacts, a restriction is added to your permit or license, and driving without those lenses is unlawful.

sec04-card-sec04-R03.front: Which letter code marks a corrective lens restriction, and what check is required to drop it?
sec04-card-sec04-R03.expected_back: Corrective lens restriction code A is added when lenses are needed to meet the minimum standard, and removing it requires a vision screening.

sec04-card-sec04-F12.front: What two steps clear a lens restriction after your eyesight improves enough to drive without glasses?
sec04-card-sec04-F12.expected_back: If your vision improves so lenses are no longer needed, you provide a new vision certificate from a licensed eye care professional and renew the license to remove the restriction.

sec04-card-sec04-F13.front: What causes driver fatigue, and which two driving abilities suffer when tiredness sets in?
sec04-card-sec04-F13.expected_back: Fatigue is physical or mental tiredness from strain, repetitive tasks, illness or lack of sleep, and it can affect vision and slow decisions.

sec04-card-sec04-F14.front: How many hours of sleep each day do most people need to stay sharp while awake?
sec04-card-sec04-F14.expected_back: Most people need seven to nine hours of sleep a day to stay properly alert during waking hours.

sec04-card-sec04-F15.front: How often should you schedule rest breaks by distance or time on a long drive?
sec04-card-sec04-F15.expected_back: On long trips, plan to stop about every one hundred miles or two hours.

sec04-card-sec04-F16.front: Besides scheduled breaks, what three precautions help prevent drowsiness on a long drive?
sec04-card-sec04-F16.expected_back: Other trip tips are bringing a companion to watch your driving, checking medicine labels for drowsiness warnings and avoiding alcohol and other drugs before or while driving.

sec04-card-sec04-F17.front: What should you do right away if tiredness hits while you are driving, and how long should a nap last?
sec04-card-sec04-F17.expected_back: If you begin to feel tired, pull off at the next exit or rest area and nap for fifteen to twenty minutes, or stop somewhere to sleep for the night.

sec04-card-sec04-F18.front: Which time of night should you avoid driving, and what is your strongest protection against fatigue?
sec04-card-sec04-F18.expected_back: Try not to drive late at night, and remember that plenty of rest is the best defense against fatigue.

sec04-card-sec04-F19.front: How does the manual define a distraction, and how risky is daydreaming compared to looking away?
sec04-card-sec04-F19.expected_back: A distraction is anything that pulls your attention from driving, and mental distractions are as dangerous as taking your eyes off the road or hands off the wheel.

sec04-card-sec04-F20.front: When does using a wireless electronic communication device behind the wheel break South Carolina law?
sec04-card-sec04-F20.expected_back: In SC it is unlawful to use a wireless electronic communication device while driving if it requires either hand, under SC Code §fifty-six-five-three thousand eight hundred ninety.

sec04-card-sec04-R05.front: What specific factor draws the legal line under South Carolina's wireless phone statute while driving?
sec04-card-sec04-R05.expected_back: The SC phone law targets devices that need the use of either hand while driving, rather than every possible phone use.

sec04-card-sec04-F21.front: What four in-cabin habits keep passengers, food, children, and pets from distracting you?
sec04-card-sec04-F21.expected_back: While driving, avoid arguments and emotional conversations with passengers, avoid eating, make sure children are buckled properly and keep pets in a carrier or portable kennel.

sec04-card-sec04-R06.front: What harm can distracted driving cause, and who holds responsibility for safe operation at all times?
sec04-card-sec04-R06.expected_back: Distracted driving can cause collisions with injury, death or property damage, and the driver remains responsible for operating the vehicle safely.

sec04-card-sec04-F22.front: What makes a driver's dangerous behavior count as aggressive driving under the manual?
sec04-card-sec04-F22.expected_back: Aggressive driving is an intentional act by a driver that endangers other people or property.

sec04-card-sec04-F23.front: Which five on-road behaviors does the manual highlight as classic aggressive driving?
sec04-card-sec04-F23.expected_back: Typical aggressive driving behaviors are speeding, tailgating, unsafe lane changes, signaling improperly or not at all, and ignoring traffic control devices.

sec04-card-sec04-R07.front: Besides speeding and tailgating, running past which four traffic controls counts as aggressive driving?
sec04-card-sec04-R07.expected_back: Speeding and tailgating are listed as aggressive behaviors, and so is failing to obey stop signs, yield signs, traffic signals or railroad crossing signals.

sec04-card-sec04-F24.front: Roughly what percentage of yearly fatal traffic crashes involve alcohol and other impairing drugs?
sec04-card-sec04-F24.expected_back: Alcohol and other impairing drugs are involved in about forty percent of traffic collisions that kill someone each year.

sec04-card-sec04-F25.front: What three alcohol actions are illegal under age twenty-one, and what kind of law covers young drivers nationwide?
sec04-card-sec04-F25.expected_back: Drivers under twenty-one may not legally buy, possess or drink alcohol, and every state has zero tolerance or similar laws for drivers under twenty-one.

sec04-card-sec04-F26.front: Why do alcohol and impairing drugs hit beginning drivers harder than seasoned motorists?
sec04-card-sec04-F26.expected_back: Alcohol and impairing drugs hit new drivers harder because they are still learning complex skills.

sec04-card-sec04-F27.front: How does the manual define judgment, and what do alcohol and impairing drugs do to it?
sec04-card-sec04-F27.expected_back: Alcohol and other impairing drugs reduce judgment, the brain's quick use of stored experience and knowledge when facing a new problem.

sec04-card-sec04-F28.front: How does alcohol distort eyesight and motion tracking, and at what BAC is every driver's vision affected?
sec04-card-sec04-F28.expected_back: Alcohol blurs vision, slows focusing, can cause double vision and weakens your judgment of distance, speed and other vehicles' movement, with vision affected at zero point zero two percent BAC for every driver.

sec04-card-sec04-F29.front: Along with blurry focus, what two critical driving abilities shrink after drinking alcohol?
sec04-card-sec04-F29.expected_back: Alcohol also reduces your ability to tell colors apart and slows your reaction time.

sec04-card-sec04-F30.front: How many drinks does it take for impairment to start and for a DUI arrest to be possible?
sec04-card-sec04-F30.expected_back: Impairment begins with the first drink, and anyone with even one drink in the bloodstream could be arrested for driving under the influence.

sec04-card-sec04-F31.front: What do the letters BAC stand for, and what ratio does that number measure?
sec04-card-sec04-F31.expected_back: BAC, blood alcohol concentration, is the percentage of alcohol relative to the amount of blood in your body.

sec04-card-sec04-R09.front: What is the manual's top rule for yourself and for friends or relatives after drinking or using drugs?
sec04-card-sec04-R09.expected_back: The manual's best advice is not to drive any vehicle after drinking alcohol or using other drugs, and never to let a friend or relative drive after drinking.

sec04-card-sec04-R12.front: According to the manual, who can drink alcohol or take impairing drugs and still operate a vehicle safely?
sec04-card-sec04-R12.expected_back: The manual says no one can drink alcohol or use other impairing drugs and still drive safely.

sec04-card-sec04-F32.front: Which three alcohol-related events can trigger suspension of your South Carolina license and driving privileges?
sec04-card-sec04-F32.expected_back: A DUI or DUAC conviction, a BAC of zero point one five percent or more, or refusing implied consent testing may lead to suspension of your license and driving privileges.

sec04-card-sec04-F33.front: How low can your BAC be and still support an impaired-driving conviction, especially if medicines are involved?
sec04-card-sec04-F33.expected_back: You can be convicted of impaired driving with a BAC of only zero point zero five, or lower when combined with drugs, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines.

sec04-card-sec04-R08.front: What happens at two hundredths, five hundredths, and fifteen hundredths percent BAC in the manual?
sec04-card-sec04-R08.memory_hook: Two blurs, five convicts, fifteen suspends
sec04-card-sec04-R08.expected_back: A BAC of zero point one five percent or more is a suspension trigger, a BAC of zero point zero five can still support an impaired-driving conviction, and zero point zero two is where vision is already affected.

sec04-card-sec04-F34.front: What immediate suspension hits a driver under twenty-one with a BAC of two hundredths percent or higher?
sec04-card-sec04-F34.expected_back: A driver under twenty-one who registers a BAC of zero point zero two percent or more has the privilege to drive suspended immediately for at least three months.

sec04-card-sec04-F35.front: How long are driving privileges immediately lost if a driver under twenty-one refuses an intoxicant check?
sec04-card-sec04-F35.memory_hook: Refuse under twenty-one, lose six months
sec04-card-sec04-F35.expected_back: A driver under twenty-one who refuses the test for intoxicants immediately loses driving privileges for at least six months.

sec04-card-sec04-F36.front: What have you agreed to in advance under South Carolina implied consent law when you accept a license?
sec04-card-sec04-F36.expected_back: Under SC's implied consent law, getting a license means you have agreed in advance to a lawful breath, blood or urine test if suspected of impaired driving, and refusing can cost you your license.

sec04-card-sec04-R10.front: Which three sample types check alcohol concentration, and how many of them can an officer require?
sec04-card-sec04-R10.expected_back: An alcohol concentration test is usually done by breath, blood or urine, and a police officer may require all three under implied consent.

sec04-card-sec04-F37.front: If you are arrested for impaired driving outside South Carolina, which state's implied consent law governs?
sec04-card-sec04-F37.expected_back: Implied consent laws differ by state, and the law of the state where you are arrested applies, not the state that issued your license.

sec04-card-sec04-F38.front: How strongly can prescription and over-the-counter medicines impair driving compared with alcohol?
sec04-card-sec04-F38.memory_hook: Medicines impair like alcohol or worse
sec04-card-sec04-F38.expected_back: Many prescription and over-the-counter drugs can affect driving as much as alcohol or worse.

sec04-card-sec04-F39.front: How do cold or allergy remedies differ from pep or diet pills in the way they hurt driving?
sec04-card-sec04-F39.memory_hook: Cold meds drowse, stimulants scramble focus
sec04-card-sec04-F39.expected_back: Over-the-counter medicines for headaches, colds, allergies or nerves can cause drowsiness, while pep pills, uppers and diet pills can cause nervousness, dizziness, poor concentration and vision problems.

sec04-card-sec04-F40.front: What two steps should you take before driving on any unfamiliar medicine?
sec04-card-sec04-F40.memory_hook: Read warnings, ask doctor or pharmacist
sec04-card-sec04-F40.expected_back: Check the label of any medicine for warnings before taking it, and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure whether it is safe to drive.

sec04-card-sec04-F41.front: How does South Carolina treat a conviction for driving under the influence of drugs?
sec04-card-sec04-F41.expected_back: A conviction in SC for driving under the influence of drugs is treated the same as a DUI or DUAC conviction.
